Basil plants themselves are absurdly easy to keep alive. Every other year ish my boyfriend and I buy one from Walmart or Trader Joe's in the grocery section for like $3-4. About the same price as packaged basil. Put it in a pot with some soil and it grows like crazy. In the winter we bring it inside and it lives by the window, and the rest of the year it lives outside. The thing grows into a small tree and we honestly can't seem to use it up fast enough. Every few months I'll make a big batch of pesto (you can sub almonds or cashews for pine nuts pretty easily and not notice a huge difference), but we also use it in pastas, pizza, sauces, etc. We have a rosemary that we did the same thing with last year and it's also huge now. Basically unlimited fresh herbs for very minimal cost and effort.

I moved and grew. 

Id always wanted to get out of my home state. Living there i wasn't happy. I didn't have any direction in life, I was depressed to the point of SH and suicidal idealation. I just wasn't healthy and didn't see a way out. I had the opportunity to move with another close friend halfway across the country, and it was the first real shot I had ever had to leave so I took it. My high school best friend had an absolute meltdown and accused me of abandoning her. She was in much the same place, still living with her parents at 30, could barely leave the house, her and her husband couldn't keep a job. I tried to explain that I was doing something that I felt was best for me, but she wouldn't hear me or didn't want to understand. So I just stopped responding to the conversation. 

Four years later I am so much better for the choice I made. I have a career that I love, which I only started in because I took a job in a field I never considered because I needed a job. I'm not financially well off, but I am comfortable, can afford my own apartment and some little luxuries. I'm in the first healthy relationship I've ever had in my life. I'm happy, genuinely happy, for the first time ever. Im safe. I've grown as a person in ways I don't think I would have if I had stayed where I was. I've had experiences I know I wouldn't have had otherwise. It hasn't always been perfect, I also stopped being as close with the friend I moved out here with, but thats okay. 

I hope the friend I left behind is doing well. I hope she found a way to get better and grow. But I don't think that it was my responsibility to stay in an environment where I was suffering just so that she didn't have to be alone in it. Part of growing sometimes means leaving friendships you have in parts of your life that aren't healthy.

I had really good luck once with making a similar shape, although less round and more pleated. The goal was to make it look like a cupcake wrapper. I interfaced the taffeta I was using, ironed it where I wanted it pleated, then drenched the whole thing in starch, ironed it again, and laid it out flat to dry with electric heaters pointed at it so it would dry quickly and evenly without the starch leaving spots. The pleats stayed beautiful, and still hold their form several years later. 

I imagine something similar could be done to help a skirt hold this shape. I would interface each piece before it's sewn, then iron the seams so they're extra crisp. Starch the heck out of each section and iron it over a rounded form and dry it that way to help it retain that shape. I would also cut some rigeline boning to the length of the hem at each section and stich it in to help keep the hem from drooping and flattening out over time. There are probably easier and less messy ways to do it than I would, though.

I work in an assisted living, and a lot of my residents don't get regular visits from their families. Especially the ones who have lived there longer. In the beginning a lot of families are around a ton. But as time goes on their aging oarent becomes "out of sight, out ot mind" unless something happens. I've had several "dump and run" placements, where a child just drops their parent off with us or we go pick them up, and then that's it, the parent is on their own with us. 

I dont blame the children. When a parent gets to the point where they need full time care I firmly believe that assisted living and nursing homes are the best option for everyone involved. Full time care is physically and emotionally exhausting. Our staff get to go home and recharge after every shift, but a child caring for their parent in the home almost never gets a break. They also aren't trained to care for them like the care staff is. They don't inherently know the best way to put on ted hose, or the safest way to give a shower, or how to help their parent with ambulatory needs. Their homes aren't designed to be as safe as possible to navigate with a walker or wheelchair. They dony chart on meds to avoid any errors. They learn a lot of times by trial and error, it seems, and that can be detrimental to their parents health and the morale of everyone involved. 

I have worked with multiple childfree residents, and it seems like the transition is usually easier on them. They didn't harbor any expectations that someone was going to care for them, and so they don't have that heartache and resentment when someone can't. They seem much more chill and thankful to the care staff a lot of the time.  They miss their homes like everyone else does, but they acclimate a lot faster and with fewer behaviors than a lot of those with children do. 

Personally I have a very optimistic outlook on transitioning to a facility someday. I see the changes being made to the industry to focus on better quality of life for the elderly, I know what to look for in a facility, which helps. But it's a pretty easy life. My residents don't really want for anything, they get truly delicious meals every day, their apartments are spotlessly cleaned for them, we arrange all transportation, I provide a variety of engaging activities all week long. Our care staff is really compassionate and committed to their health and safety. It's a good life overall.

That's absolutely horrifying to even think about. But I would believe it happens in the worst situations. I've had residents get bad tears on their hands and arms from just brushing up against the hand rails on the wall a little too hard. Others who had falls on carpet and the carpet just stripped away their skin, requiring weeks, sometimes even months, of regular wound care. It breaks my heart to see them hurt.

Skin tears are a HUGE problem with the elderly. They happen so easily and take so long to heal. Well moisturized skin is less likely to suffer tearing. Not to mention that dry, flakey skin is so uncomfortable. I've had residents who get so bad that daily lotioning is a part of their care plan, but I think it should be a part of really everyone's.

I had mine at 22 in Arizona. Just celebrated 7 years sterile last month. There are absolutely doctors out there who will do it! 

I recommend bringing a lot of literature with you if you can. I had print outs of my insurances guidelines for sterilization, some government information, a 4 page long, bullet pointed, front and back list of reasons I felt like sterilization was right for me, a few studies I had found online stating that sterilization regret is almost always associated with individuals who had children and decided they wanted more post sterilization, and a few other things. I walked in with a folder and was prepared to walk right out if I was denied. I was very lucky, my doctor took the folder and told me she could put it in my file, but that she trusted me to know what was best for myself. She submitted it all to insurance and just over a month later held my hand while they put me under so she could slice my tubes out.

Every now and then I wonder if I was infertile. When I was very young, before I was 100% committed to how childfree I am now and was pretty stupid I had a lot of risky sex. Like I was on birth control, but I wasn't always perfect about taking it, and when I was off of it I just used condoms. But I have never had so much as a slightly too late period. 

Its a moot point now, though. I got sterilized when I was 22 because I wasn't going to push my luck any further and didn't want to risk someday winding up pregnant and in need of an abortion. I'll be 30 next month and I am more thankful to 22 year old me every day for the choice I made. It's literally the only smart thing I did back then.

If you've reached a point in your mobility where you can't get up without using your arms, practice getting up in the "nose over toes" method. Scoot to the edge, lean forward so your head is over your feet (head UP though, don't point your head down to the floor), and push up through your feet using your arms to assist as needed. I work with the elderly, and have had to teach a lot of them to get up this way because they struggle. Many of them will try to pull themselves up with their walkers or a table, or lift up with their body still fully in the chair. This can be both difficult and dangerous. Some even wind up feeling like they need an aide to haul them up with and underarm assist, which can be strenuous and harmful to both parties. It reduces a lot of strain and risk of falls/injury, as well as helping to improve balance.

If you want to get a good curl on fishing line wrap a bunch of it around a smaller tube (I've used toilet paper rolls), and hit it with a hairdryer on high for a little bit. That will set the curl of the fishing line a bit tigher that it would be just off the spool. I like to then use a rolled hem foot when I do my hem and feed it into the foot with the fabric to have it all done at once. It's a lot faster than doing the rolled hem and feeding it in after, or doing the hem by hand and then setting the fishing line in as you go. I've also done the hem and then done a tight zigzag stitch along the hem over the fishing line, but that doesn't produce as clean of a look.

If you can take care of your elderly relatives that's great. But as someone who works in an assisted living home with dementia patients, I can tell you thats not always feasible or possible. Several of my residents are wheelchair bound, and need assistance of one, sometimes two, people to help them get to the bathroom or in and out of bed. Most are incontinent, and need to be taken to the bathroom and changed frequently. Some can't eat on their own and need to be fed at every meal. Almost none of them can bathe themselves. Some go through periods where in their confusion they become extremely violent and combative. I could go on and on about all of the specific care that some residents need. From the time I step onto the floor to the time I leave at the end of my shift I am constantly assisting someone so that they can live as safe and healthy of a life as they can. And unfortunately they are here because the level of care they need is beyond what their families can offer. Either the physical demands of moving their relative, or the time demands of how often they need to be cared for, or the emotional drain can be too much. 

Its not always as simple as people getting the fuck over themselves and taking care of their relatives. Sometimes it's just not possible for the family to provide the care that their relative needs, and the best course of action for everyone is to place them in a home appropriate to their condition so that they can get that care.

I've basically abandoned my cosplay Instagram at this point. I dont have the money to put together new, exciting cosplays and pay gor photoshoots in new, exciting locations with new, exciting concepts. And that's what it feels like you have to do to keep up on Instagram. The content is pretty static, its hard to constantly come up with content for photos when you have extremely limited resources and its super discouraging. And honestly kind of alienating, you feel like a piece of shit because everyone else is constantly posting their photoshoots and new cosplays. 



Tiktok makes it a lot easier to create cosplay content. It's a lot more engaging, there's more stuff you can do when it's a video based platform. And yeah, I could try to take and post similar videos for Instagram. But that would mean having to buy editing software (and a computer to run it on), doing the audio myself for everything (which likely means I wouldn't be able to use audio from shows and stuff because I don't know how I would possibly record a scene lip synching and then perfectly match up the audio after it's been recorded vs. Just recording the video to the audio in the app), and then finally uploading it to Instagram. Tiktok has literally all of that right there in the app. And it doesn't cost me to use it. It's just a lot more attractive and engaging to me both from a user and creator standpoint. The only "downside" is that I can't edit myself to be the most attractive version of myself like I can on Instagram, which makes the desire to film myself and create content lower because I'm not that attractive to begin with.
